exclusions.because: A record or an enum carries values across a seam and hides nothing behind them. Its interface is its content, so a score would only say how many fields it has, and ranking them beside the modules that do hide something would bury the finding.

A Spring Data repository interface has no implementation written in this repository: the query is derived from the method name and the code is generated at run time. Scoring it would measure a naming convention rather than anything anybody wrote.
The application's entry point exists to be started, not to be called. Its one method has the signature the platform dictates, and no module inside the application ever learns it.

reach.adapter: An interface whose implementation Spring Data generates at run time is how this application reaches its database. A module that drives one coordinates storage its caller never has to open, which is the plainest kind of reach there is.
reach.persistentRecord: A type marked as an entity is a row that outlives the call it was written in. A module reaching one is keeping a record on its caller's behalf: it decides what goes into it, and the caller learns neither the table nor the identifier it was written under.
reach.transaction: A module that marks itself or one of its methods transactional establishes the transaction its whole flow runs in. That is the one piece of coordination a caller most obviously does not do: they make one call, and either all of what it set in motion happened or none of it did.

refusals.because: A refusal a module can answer with is something its caller has to know before they call it: it decides what they write around the call, and a caller who does not know about it has not learned the module. So it is charged a weight of its own, and charged it whatever the refusal is called: the types every caller already knows are types they already hold, and knowing that IllegalStateException exists is not the same as knowing that this module can answer with one, which is the thing being learned here. It is then reported as a band of its own, so that a module whose interface is wide because it is honest about how it can fail can be told apart from one that is merely wide. Folded into a single number the two are identical, and a module is paid for saying nothing about its failure modes.

documentedNeverRaised.because: The module's own documentation promises a refusal that nothing in its implementation can throw. Whoever reads the seam writes a catch for something that will never arrive, and whatever the module does refuse for arrives under some other name. Either the documentation is stale or the code lost a check, and which of the two it is is a question for a person; that there is a disagreement is a question for a machine.

raisedNeverDocumented.because: The implementation throws a refusal the module's documentation never mentions. A caller reading the seam finds nothing to catch, and meets it at run time instead. This is the cheaper of the two to fix and the more expensive to be handed by a customer.

notRead.because: The graph covers the application's own source and nothing else. Test code is written to check a module rather than to be one, so scoring it would measure the checking; build output is derived from source that has already been read, so it would draw the same module twice; and an installed dependency is somebody else's source, which nobody in this repository can act on and which would arrive by the tens of thousands of files. Each would put modules on the page that nobody here wrote, and the finding would be buried under them. A directory is named outright and never walked into, which is what keeps a node_modules to one line in the graph instead of everything inside it; a file is matched on what its name ends with, which is how both languages here spell a test and how TypeScript spells a generated declaration. The names here are ones nothing but a tool ever writes: a bare test or tests is deliberately not among them, because that is a legal Java package name and a rule that quietly took a package of the application's own source off the page would be worse than one that misses a directory somebody can add to this list.

readAt.says: A Java module is a class, because that is where a Java interface is written.
A TypeScript module is a file, because that is what an import names and so is the whole of what a caller of one gets.
